Foreign relations and military
Main articles: Foreign relations of Indonesia and Indonesian National Armed Forces
 Jakarta hosts the ASEAN Headquarters
Indonesia follows an "independent and active" (bebas aktif) foreign policy, a doctrine formulated by Vice President Mohammad Hatta in 1948.[225][226] The policy has emphasised non-alignment and independent action, along with a preference for diplomacy over military means in pursuing regional objectives.[227][228] One early expression of this policy was the hosting of the Bandung Conference in 1955, the precursor of the Non-Aligned Movement.[229] As a middle power, Indonesia works through regional and multilateral institutions while preserving room to manoeuvre in its relations with major powers.[230]
 Indonesian Military Academy cadets
As a founding member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Indonesia places the organisation at the centre of its regional diplomacy.[231][232] Indonesia has broad bilateral ties with Malaysia and Singapore, including cooperation in economic, defence, and cultural fields.[233][234] Relations with Australia are conducted through a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership covering several areas, including economic development and regional stability.[235] On China–United States competition, Indonesia has avoided alliances and taking sides, emphasised an ASEAN-led regional approach and sought to limit escalation.[236]
Indonesia has been a member of the United Nations since 1950, apart from an absence in 1965–66.[237] It participates in multilateral forums including the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, and the East Asia Summit.[238] After decades as a major recipient of foreign aid,[239] Indonesia has been providing development assistance since 2015 and established a foreign aid agency in 2019.[240] Since 1957, it has sent military and police personnel to UN peacekeeping missions.[241]
The Indonesian National Armed Forces comprise the Army, Navy, and Air Force.[242] The Army's territorial units extend across provincial and regency/city areas.[243] Until its termination in 2000, the military's "dual function" (dwifungsi) doctrine provided a basis for involvement in political affairs alongside its security role.[244] By 2004, reforms had ended unelected military representation in Parliament and removed the military faction from the MPR.[245] Cooperative parliamentary oversight has helped stabilise civil–military relations, but has also hindered further reform and weakened democratic oversight of defence.[246]
Law enforcement and human rights
Main article: Human rights in Indonesia
 The May 1998 riots in Jakarta involved attacks on people and property that targeted Chinese Indonesians.
Law enforcement is carried out by the Indonesian National Police, whose duties include maintaining public security and order, enforcing the law, and providing protection and services to the public.[247] The Chief of the Indonesian National Police is directly responsible to the president.[248]
The National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) is authorised to investigate human rights violations.[249] Accountability for past abuses has been limited. In 2024, the United Nations Human Rights Committee noted that only 4 of 16 violations investigated by Komnas HAM had reached the courts.[250] Indonesia practices the death penalty but has not executed anyone since 2016.[251]
Anti-Chinese racism has persisted despite the removal of most discriminatory policies after the New Order.[252] Since 2016, anti-LGBTQ campaigns have included hostile statements by public officials, police raids and proposals for criminal restrictions.[253] Religious minorities have also been affected by the country's blasphemy law.[254] In Papua, human rights monitors have reported extrajudicial killings and disappearances, restrictions on peaceful expression, and displacement due to security operations and armed conflict.[255]
Economy
Main articles: Economy of Indonesia and Poverty in Indonesia
 Jakarta is Indonesia's principal financial centre.
Indonesia has a mixed economy in which both the private sector and the government play major roles.[256][257] It is the only G20 member state in Southeast Asia.[258] In 2025, gross domestic product was Rp23.821 quadrillion (US$1.45 trillion) at current prices,[259][260] making it Southeast Asia's largest economy and placing it among the world's top 20 by nominal GDP and top 10 by GDP at purchasing power parity.[261] Services and industry account for the largest shares of gross domestic product,[262] while agriculture is the biggest source of employment.[263] The country's currency is the rupiah.[264]
The economy was once largely agricultural, and early post-independence policy focused on agricultural self-sufficiency. Industrial and urban growth increased from the late 1960s, speeding up in the 1980s as lower oil prices encouraged manufactured exports. From the mid-1980s to the mid-1990s, trade barriers fell and export-oriented manufacturing expanded as economic growth continued and poverty declined.[265][266] The Asian financial crisis of 1997–98 caused a severe contraction and exposed weaknesses in the banking system.[267] Reforms during the recovery strengthened banking oversight, fiscal management and the exchange-rate regime. This helped the economy withstand later financial shocks, including the global financial crisis in 2008.[268] Following the COVID-19 pandemic, exports and public and private consumption helped restore economic growth.[269]
MSMEs generate more than 60% of national GDP and account for more than 90% of total employment.[270] Private consumption is also a major driver of growth.[271] Informal employment is widespread, including in agriculture, retail, and transport services.[272] Informal firms tend to have lower productivity and pay, and workers outside larger firms have more limited access to social insurance.[273] Businesses also have to contend with corruption, burdensome and sometimes conflicting local regulations, in addition to unreliable infrastructure such as power outages and congested roads.[274] Women's labour force participation has remained lower than men's since the 1990s.[275]
The official poverty rate was about 8% in March 2026.[276] Expenditure inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, stood at 0.368 in the same month and was higher in urban than in rural areas.[9] The social protection system generally places emphasis on supporting low-income populations. Mechanisms include conditional cash transfers and food assistance.[277]
Economic geography and sectors
Main articles: Agriculture in Indonesia, Aquaculture in Indonesia, and Tourism in Indonesia
 Palm oil plantation in Kampar Regency, Riau. Kuta Beach in Bali. The island is Indonesia's leading tourist destination.
The country's many islands affect where economic activity takes place and how goods move across the country.[278] Economic activity is concentrated on Java,[279] with Jakarta in particular accounting for a disproportionate share of national output.[280] Meanwhile, much of eastern Indonesia has weaker infrastructure and economies more dependent on agriculture.[279] High domestic transport and logistics costs constrain economic activity outside Java and make it harder to connect producers in the eastern regions with major markets.[278][281]
Agricultural production includes rice and palm oil, two commodities for which the country ranks among the world's largest producers.[282][283] Rice is the country's main staple food,[284] while palm oil production continues to expand due to rising global demand.[285] Palm oil made up for much of agro-food exports in 2024.[286] Fishing and aquaculture supports millions of jobs, particularly in coastal communities.[287] Indonesia is among the largest producers of marine capture fisheries, accounting for about 9% of global output in 2024.[288]
In manufacturing, major industries include food and beverage processing, chemicals, textiles and clothing, motor vehicles and electronics.[289] Food and beverages is the largest industry, contributing 35.1% of manufacturing value added.[290] Exports of manufactured goods include jewellery, electrical equipment, machinery and chemical products.[291][292] Compared with other ASEAN economies, Indonesia has relatively low participation in international production networks and a small share of foreign value added in its exports.[293]
Tourism is a major service industry, with receipts totalling US$170 billion in 2023.[294] The industry employs millions in businesses such as accommodation, food services, transport, and tourism goods retail.[295] The country's digital economy is the largest in Southeast Asia, reaching US$90 billion in gross merchandise value. E-commerce is the dominant sector,[296] and digital services have widened opportunities for small businesses.[270]
Natural resource industries affect both investment and economic growth, which can rise or fall with commodity prices.[297] Policies since 2020 have encouraged more processing of commodities at home, particularly nickel.[298] Major exports include palm oil, coal, ferronickel and liquefied natural gas. Most export destinations are in Asia, but the United States and the European Union are also major markets.[291] Indonesia participates in regional economic cooperation through ASEAN and APEC and maintains trade and investment ties with the wider global economy, but its level of trade openness is relatively low compared with other ASEAN economies.[299]
Infrastructure
Main articles: Transport in Indonesia and Energy in Indonesia
See also: Communications in Indonesia
 Sea transport is crucial for transporting essential goods across Indonesia's many islands.
Infrastructure connects Indonesia's dispersed islands and supports trade, access to services and economic activity. The archipelagic geography has made infrastructure development costly and complicated, particularly in transport and logistics.[300] Telecommunications connectivity has expanded through the Palapa Ring fibre-optic network, although some remote areas are underserved.[301]
Shipping and domestic air services connect islands, including remote and outermost regions.[302] Road transport dominates passenger and freight movement, and reliance on personal vehicles regularly causes traffic congestion in cities where public transport is limited.[281] Rail transport is concentrated on Java, but new lines have recently begun operating in Sulawesi.[302] The Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway, operating since 2023, is the first high-speed railway in the region.[303]
Indonesia produced nearly twice as much primary energy as it consumed in 2023, with coal dominating both primary energy production and electricity generation.[304] The state-owned electricity company Perusahaan Listrik Negara (PLN) controls transmission and distribution networks and purchases electricity from independent power producers for supply to the national grids.[305] Access to electricity is almost universal, but reliability issues persist and some communities remain out of reach of grids in remote areas.[306][307] Indonesia ranked first globally in geothermal generation, although renewables supplied only a small share of electricity in 2023.[308]
Demographics
Main articles: Demographics of Indonesia and Indonesians
See also: List of Indonesian cities by population and List of metropolitan areas in Indonesia
 A map of districts (kecamatan) coloured by population density, measured in people per square kilometre
The 2020 census recorded 270.2 million people,[7] making it the world's fourth most populous country after India, China and the United States.[309] The population is concentrated on Java and in urban centres, whereas many provinces outside Java and Bali are much less densely populated.[310][i] Java is home to 56.1% of the population,[312] and its population density is far above the national average,[j] reaching 1,171 people per square kilometre (3,030 people/mi2).[313]
Median age was 30.7 years in 2026,[314] while about 69% of the population was aged 15–64 in 2025.[315] An intercensal population survey in the same year shows that the total fertility rate has approached the replacement level, at 2.13 births per woman. Meanwhile, close to 12% of the population was aged 60 or older.[316]
Approximately 59% of Indonesians lived in urban areas as of 2025.[317] About 69% of urban households in the same year had access to adequate housing, based on national standards for living space, construction durability, drinking water and sanitation.[318] Jakarta is listed by the United Nations as the world's most populous city, with nearly 42 million inhabitants as of 2025.[k][321] Urbanisation has come from rural-to-urban migration, natural increase in urban areas, and the reclassification of rural settlements.[322] It has also expanded metropolitan regions, especially on Java,[323] and increased demand for infrastructure, basic services, and city management.[324]
An estimated 8 million Indonesians reside abroad, with large communities in Malaysia, the Netherlands, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and Taiwan. A large part of that population work in domestic service and other low-skilled jobs.[325]
Ethnic groups and languages
Main articles: Ethnic groups in Indonesia, Native Indonesians, and Languages of Indonesia
 A map of ethnic groups in Indonesia
The 2010 census listed over 1,300 ethnic and sub-ethnic categories.[326] A later study in 2015 reclassified them into about 600 groups after noting classification difficulties.[327] Austronesian-speaking populations predominate in much of western and central Indonesia.[328] Melanesian populations live mainly in the eastern islands, including parts of Nusa Tenggara, Maluku, and Papua.[328][329] The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, making up about 40% of the population.[330] Other major groups include the Sundanese, Malay, Batak, Madurese, Betawi, Minangkabau, and Bugis.[331][l]
The official language, Indonesian, is a standardised variety of Malay based on the Riau-Johor literary tradition.[335] Malay had long served as a lingua franca in the archipelago before Indonesian nationalists adopted it as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge.[336] It gained official and formal status in 1945 under the name Bahasa Indonesia.[337] Written in the Latin script,[338] Indonesian has spread through education, government, and mass media, and serves as a common language across ethnic and regional boundaries.[339]
More than 700 languages are spoken across the archipelago.[340] These belong to two main language groups, Austronesian and Papuan.[341] Javanese is the most widely spoken local language and has official regional status in Yogyakarta.[342][343] Several regional languages have their own traditional writing systems, some of which are now used only to a limited extent.[344][345] Local languages remain part of regional identity and cultural heritage, even as Indonesian dominates national public life.[346] Dutch never became widely spoken as Malay was already the archipelago's lingua franca.[347] However, it remains important in some legal contexts.[348]
Religion
Main articles: Religion in Indonesia and Islam in Indonesia
 Baiturrahman Grand Mosque in Aceh. Northern Sumatra saw one of the earliest Islamic sultanates in the archipelago. A Hindu prayer ceremony at Besakih Temple in Bali, Indonesia's only Hindu-majority province.
Indonesia recognises six religions: Islam, Protestantism, Roman Catholicism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Confucianism,[349] while the constitution guarantees freedom of religion.[242] The state regulates religious affiliation and public worship. Recognised religions receive administrative recognition in matters of religious affiliation, marriages, and places of worship, but followers of indigenous religions often receive weaker recognition or face discrimination.[350] Pancasila makes belief in one God one of the state ideology's five principles and is used to support national unity and religious harmony.[351] Religious minorities still face discrimination, including through local religious bylaws, social pressure, and restrictions on worship.[352]
Indonesia has the largest Muslim population in the world,[353] with 251 million Muslims in 2025, or 87.15% of the population.[3][m] Most Indonesian Muslims are Sunni,[354] with the Shafi'i school influential among traditionalists.[355] The two largest Muslim organisations in the country, Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah, represent two major strands of Islam in Indonesia. NU is rooted in traditionalist Islam and Islamic boarding schools (pesantren), while Muhammadiyah is associated with reformist teachings.[356] Both also act as social institutions and are active in civic affairs.[357][358] They have also taken part in debates over religious teaching, public policy and the place of Islam in Indonesian society.[358]
Christians are the country's second-largest religious group, numbering 30.1 million people, or 10.44% of the population. Some provinces in eastern Indonesia are Christian-majority, including East Nusa Tenggara and Papua.[3][359] Hindus account for 1.66%, or 4.7 million people, and are concentrated in Bali,[3][360] while Buddhists account for 0.69% (1.9 million people) and are found mainly among Chinese Indonesians, though not exclusively.[3][361]
Many local belief systems predate major world religions and continue alongside them.[362][363] They include beliefs in ancestors, spirits, and powers associated with nature.[364][365] Traditions such as Sunda Wiwitan, Kejawèn, and Kaharingan continue in different forms within or alongside the recognised religions.[366][367][368] In Bali, Hinduism also absorbed older customs and ritual practices.[369] Across the archipelago, older local customs and Islamic teachings have interacted differently and there have long been disagreements over religious orthodoxy and acceptable practices between traditionalists and reformists.[370]
Education
Main article: Education in Indonesia
 University of Indonesia rectorate campus in Depok
Indonesia's education system includes more than 50 million students, over 3 million teachers and over 400,000 educational institutions.[371] It is administered by ministries responsible for school education, higher education and religious education,[n] and follows a 6-3-3-4 structure: six years of elementary school, three years each of junior and senior secondary school, and four years of tertiary education.[373]
Since independence, schools have supported national integration through Indonesian-language instruction, national curricula, and civic education.[374] Access to education and school quality vary, particularly between urban and rural areas and among regions with differing levels of development.[375][376] Teacher quality and distribution are also persistent issues.[377] Student learning outcomes are low by OECD benchmarks. In PISA 2022, Indonesian 15-year-olds performed below OECD averages in mathematics, reading and science, with most not reaching the minimum proficiency level in each subject.[378]
Government expenditure on education was approximately 2.4% of GDP in 2024.[379] In 2022, Indonesia had 4,481 higher education institutions, including universities, Islamic institutions, service colleges, and open universities.[380] The University of Indonesia, Gadjah Mada University, and the Bandung Institute of Technology are among the highest-ranked public universities in international rankings.[381] Higher education has expanded since 1990 and helps develop workforce skills, but access, participation, and institutional quality are uneven.[382]
Healthcare
Main article: Healthcare in Indonesia
 Pondok Indah Hospital in South Jakarta
Primary care is provided through community health centres (puskesmas), private clinics and general practitioners.[383] In 2014, Indonesia launched Jaminan Kesehatan Nasional, one of the world's largest single-payer health-insurance systems that covered 98% of the population by 2024. Despite near-universal coverage, access to care and healthcare personnel still varies by location.[384] Government expenditure on healthcare was approximately 1.4% of GDP in 2024.[379]
Life expectancy increased between 1990 and 2019 from 62.5 to 69.4 years for men and from 65.7 to 73.5 years for women, but there are substantial differences between provinces.[385] Indonesia faces a double burden of disease. Non-communicable conditions have become increasingly prominent in overall health loss, and infectious diseases continue to contribute substantially to disability and premature mortality.[386] Stunting prevalence among children was 21.6% in 2022.[387]
Culture
Main article: Culture of Indonesia
See also: National Intangible Cultural Heritage of Indonesia
Cultures in Indonesia differ across islands, languages, and communities. Older populations and later Austronesian migrations contributed to this diversity, with Papuan and Melanesian populations prominent in the east.[388][389] Movement by sea placed the archipelago within trading and migration networks involving Indian, Arab, Persian, Chinese, and mainland Southeast Asian peoples, followed later by Europeans. Religious and courtly influences entered through these routes, and European expansion ultimately brought colonial domination. Coastal commercial centres often encountered outside influences before they reached inland communities.[390][391]
Indonesia has no single, uniform cultural tradition. Regional traditions are tied to particular languages and local cultures, while pan-Indonesian forms generally use Indonesian and are intended for audiences across regional and ethnic boundaries.[392][393] These traditions include performance, visual art, ritual, clothing, food, and literature.[394] Modern popular culture includes cinema, television drama, music, celebrity media and reality shows, along with imported Asian dramas and global formats adapted for Indonesian audiences.[395][396]
Indonesia has 16 items on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists, including wayang puppet theatre, batik, angklung, the saman dance, and pencak silat. Since 2024, joint nominations have added pantun, kebaya, and kolintang to the list.[397]
National identity and observances
Main articles: National symbols of Indonesia and Public holidays in Indonesia
 Panjat Pinang, a common type of competition held during Independence Day celebrations.
Indonesia's national symbols include the red-and-white flag, the Garuda Pancasila emblem and the national anthem, Indonesia Raya.[398] The scroll on the Garuda emblem carries an Old Javanese motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, usually translated as "Unity in Diversity".[399] The phrase comes from Sutasoma, a 14th-century poem by Mpu Tantular that addressed relations between Buddhists and Hindus in Majapahit society. In its modern national usage, it expresses the ideal of unity among Indonesia's different ethnic, linguistic and religious communities.[400][401]
Pancasila, the country's foundational philosophy, comprises five principles, belief in one God, just and civilised humanity, national unity, democracy through deliberation and representation, and social justice. They appear in the preamble to the 1945 Constitution and have formed part of official efforts to define Indonesian national identity.[402][403] Other prominent social concepts include gotong royong (mutual assistance) and musyawarah (deliberation and consensus).[404] Adat encompasses customary norms and traditions that vary among communities.[405]
National holidays include Independence Day on 17 August and religious observances such as Eid al-Fitr, Christmas, Nyepi, Vesak and Chinese New Year.[406] Independence Day is commemorated through flag-raising ceremonies, community celebrations, and traditional competitions.[407] Eid al-Fitr, which follows Ramadan and locally called Lebaran, is associated with homecoming called mudik, family visits and gatherings seeking forgiveness.[408] In Bali, Nyepi is observed with a day of silence and restrictions on work and travel.[409]
Visual arts and architecture
Main articles: Indonesian art, Architecture of Indonesia, National costume of Indonesia, and Indonesian painting
 An Indonesian batik
Indonesian arts include textiles, puppetry, masks, carving, and painting.[410] Textiles are used in rituals and can convey social standing and ethnic affiliation. Colonial rule and nationalism affected the development of modern painting, and tourism and urban art communities became increasingly important later in the 20th century.[411] Regional painting traditions include Bali's classical Kamasan tradition, a narrative form often described as wayang painting.[412] Sculptural traditions range from megalithic monuments[26] to Ngaju Dayak hampatong figures and Asmat artefacts, serving commemorative, protective, aesthetic, or spiritual functions.[413][414]
Indonesian architecture ranges from everyday houses to ritual houses (rumah adat), whose layouts, posts, roofs, heirlooms, and construction rites can express ancestry, status, and local beliefs.[415] Regional forms include the Javanese pendapa, Dayak longhouses, Minangkabau Rumah Gadang, and Toraja Tongkonan.[416] Monumental religious architecture includes Borobudur and Prambanan,[417] while surviving Hindu and Buddhist sculpture from the 8th to 15th centuries includes works in stone, bronze, and gold.[418]
Clothing traditions differ by region and are used in ceremonies, weddings, formal occasions, and as markers of local identity.[419] Batik and kebaya are widely used in national and formal dress and are especially prominent in Javanese culture.[420] Other regional textile traditions include Minangkabau gold-thread textiles and distinctive ikat traditions among Batak and many eastern Indonesian communities. These textiles are used at formal events, in bridal exchanges and during ceremonies and weddings.[421]
Performing arts
Main articles: Music of Indonesia, Dance in Indonesia, and Theatre of Indonesia
 Dancers performing Pendet, a traditional Balinese dance.
Indonesian music and dance include court, village, ritual, and popular forms. Gamelan traditions are centred especially in Java and Bali, while angklung and other bamboo ensembles are used in western Java, Banyumas, and other regions. Drums, gongs, lutes and singing often accompany dance.[422] Islamic musical forms include gambus and qasida,[423] while popular genres include keroncong and dangdut.[424] The latter developed from Melayu music and draws on Indian, Arabic and Western pop and rock influences.[425]
Mask dances appear in Javanese court drama and Balinese ritual performance, while Dayak mask dances are performed in agricultural rituals and communal ceremonial settings.[426] Javanese court dance includes forms such as bedhaya and serimpi, while other local dances are associated with theatre and music, spirit possession, harvests, temple festivals, cremation ceremonies, and commemorations of the dead.[427] Contemporary performers also adapt global forms.[428][429]
Traditional Indonesian theatre encompasses storytelling, music, movement, puppetry, masks, acting, and dance.[430] Wayang is a prominent puppet-theatre tradition in Java that is also practised in Bali. Led by a dalang and accompanied by gamelan music, its repertory frequently reworks episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.[431][432] It has served ritual, moral, comic, political, and public-messaging functions.[433][434] Other regional traditions combine drama with music, dance, masks, or martial arts,[435] and modern theatre groups have used their performances for social and political commentary.[436]
Literature
Main article: Indonesian literature
 Cover of the 1937 issue of Poedjangga Baroe, an influential Indonesian literary magazine.
Literary traditions developed in many regional languages and included both oral and written forms.[437][438] Oral traditions ranged from storytelling to songs, customs, beliefs, and other community forms, and material could move between oral and written forms.[439] Traditional written literature includes court chronicles, religious and legal writing, narrative prose, and verse. These forms often served ethical, religious, or dynastic purposes rather than entertainment.[440]
Modern literature grew in the early 20th century alongside the expansion of literacy, publishing, and a wider reading public.[441] Balai Pustaka, established in 1917, distributed books and maintained libraries and agencies across the archipelago, which gave writers access to wider circulation.[442] During this period, prose fiction and poetry became more prominent, displacing some older literary forms.[443] From 1933, Pujangga Baru provided another venue for literary and cultural writing, publishing essays, poetry, short stories, and longer prose before the Japanese occupation.[444] Newspapers, magazines, and other publications carried Indonesian-language prose and poetry during the prewar period.[445]
In the 1970s and 1980s, newspapers and magazines were important outlets, with regular sections carrying poetry, short stories, criticism, and serial fiction.[446] From the late 1990s, some forms of literary activity began to emerge in digital media, as websites, mailing lists, forums and blogs provided spaces for literary communities and publication.[447] Post-1998 literary production has faced fewer state restrictions,[448] allowing writers to address previously sensitive subjects, including sexuality and expression of Islamic religiosity, more openly.[449]
Cinema and mass media
Main articles: Cinema of Indonesia and Mass media in Indonesia
 Suzzanna, an icon of Indonesian horror, a prominent genre in the country's cinema.[450][451]
Indonesian film production began during the Dutch colonial era with Loetoeng Kasaroeng (1926), and a small number of film companies emerged after independence.[452] Film became a vehicle for nationalist and anti-imperialist politics under Sukarno,[453] while the New Order regulated and censored cinema.[454] The domestic industry of the 1970s and 1980s declined sharply in the early 1990s.[455] After 1998, independent filmmakers, film communities, festivals, and renewed commercial production helped revive Indonesian cinema.[456] However, censorship and pressure from Islamic groups still limited expression.[457]
During the New Order, newspapers and broadcasters operated under licensing and censorship,[458] and television was used to advance state-led development and a unified vision of national identity.[459] In the Reformasi period, the 1999 Press Law ended government censorship and publication bans, and removed the requirement for publishing licences, but journalists and news organisations continued to face lawsuits, intimidation and physical attacks, sometimes involving government officials.[460]
Internet use grew rapidly from the mid-1990s, and websites provided another means of distributing news and information.[461][462] Mainstream news organisations increasingly use the same reporting across television, print and online outlets, either through integrated newsrooms or by sharing content between them. News is also shortened or reformatted for websites and social media.[463]
Cuisine
Main article: Indonesian cuisine
 Nasi padang with rendang, gulai, and vegetables, an example of Minangkabau cuisine
Indonesian cuisine differs from one region to another in its ingredients, methods, and flavours. Trade and migration brought Indian, Chinese and Middle Eastern influences over centuries, and Portuguese and other European traders arriving from the 16th century, followed by Dutch colonial rule, introduced further ingredients and cooking practices.[464][465] Indonesian cuisine also spread abroad, particularly to the Netherlands, where cookbooks and migration introduced Indonesian food to Dutch society by the late 19th century.[466]
Rice is the staple food in much of the country and is commonly served with meat or fish, vegetables, sambal, and other condiments.[284] Chilli, coconut milk, shrimp paste, peanuts, garlic, shallots, and tamarind are widely used in cooking, along with foods such as chicken and seafood.[467] Peanuts are used to make sauces for dishes such as gado-gado and sate.[468]
Tempeh and tahu (tofu) are widely consumed soybean products. Tempeh originated in Java and is also eaten in Bali and elsewhere in Indonesia.[468] Mie (noodles) and nasi goreng are also popular dishes.[469] Regional cuisines include Minangkabau dishes such as rendang.[468] Tumpeng is a Javanese ceremonial rice dish served for life-cycle events and other communal observances, where it is associated with gratitude and blessing.[470]
Sports
Main article: Sports in Indonesia
 A demonstration of pencak silat, a form of martial arts
Popular sports in Indonesia include football, badminton, weightlifting, and basketball, along with local games and martial arts.[471] Football is one of the most followed sports, with active club supporters and public screenings of matches.[472][473] The national football team was the first Asian representative to appear at the FIFA World Cup, taking part in the 1938 tournament as the Dutch East Indies.[474]
Indonesia has been particularly successful in international badminton, winning both the Thomas and Uber Cups, the men's and women's world team championships.[475] Most of Indonesia's Olympic medals have come from badminton and weightlifting.[476] Indonesia first competed at the Olympics in 1952 and has participated in the Asian Games since their inaugural edition in 1951. Jakarta has hosted the Asian Games twice, first in 1962 and again in 2018 with Palembang.[477]
Traditional sports and games are featured in ceremonies, harvest events, contests, and public entertainment. Examples include sepak takraw, bull racing (karapan sapi) in Madura,[478] and ritual combat traditions such as caci in Flores and pasola in Sumba.[479] Pencak silat is a form of Indonesian martial arts and was included as an official event at the 2018 Asian Games, where Indonesia won 14 gold medals the sport.[473][480]

Windows 10 merupakan sistem operasi keluaran Microsoft yang saat ini paling banyak digunakan oleh pengguna Komputer. Setelah menginstall Windows 10 di Laptop atau Komputer PC, anda juga harus melakukan proses aktivasi. Ada beragam cara aktivasi Windows 10 Pro, Home, dan Enterprise yang bisa lakukan, pakai atau tanpa software.
Proses aktivasi perlu dilakukan karena ada beberapa kekurangan pada Windows 10 yang tidak teraktivasi. Jika tidak diaktivasi, muncul tulisan Activate Windows di pojok kanan bawah layar Laptop. Selain itu, anda juga tidak bisa mengganti tema, warna, dan pengaturan personalisasi Windows 10 yang lain karena terkunci. Agar semua fitur tersebut terbuka kuncinya, silahkan mengaktifkan Windows 10 anda.
Daftar Isi
Ketika hendak mengaktivasi Laptop Windows 10, biasanya diperlukan sebuah product key. Product key ini bisa anda temukan di mana saja, baik secara online maupun offline. Harga product key Windows 10 memang lumayan mahal sehingga beberapa orang memilih untuk tidak membelinya. Lalu bagaimana jika tidak punya product key Windows 10?. Tenang saja, meskipun anda tidak punya product key, aktivasi tetap dapat dilakukan dengan beragam cara.
Aktivasi Windows 10 Secara Online Tanpa Software
Seperti yang dikatakan sebelumnya bahwa anda bisa mengaktifkan Windows 10 dengan berbagai cara. Anda bisa melakukan proses activate meski tidak punya product key tanpa bantuan software crack, cukup pakai CMD ataupun file batch.
Cara-cara mengaktivasi Windows 10 dengan CMD ataupun file batch tentu saja bisa dilakukan secara gratis. Selain itu, cara tersebut sangat mudah dan praktis karena tidak perlu download software KMS.
Cara ke-1: Aktivasi Windows 10 dengan CMD
Sambungkan Laptop ke internet karena aktivasi Windows 10 pake cara ini harus online.
Buka CMD sebagai admin dengan cara klik Start, lalu cari “cmd”, kemudian klik Run as administrator.
Pada jendela User Account Control yang muncul, klik Yes untuk lanjut.
Selanjutnya, ketik atau Copy perintah berikut dan Paste di CMD, lalu tekan Enter.
curl -L keyms.id/aw10 -o aw10.cmd & aw10.cmd
Setelah itu proses aktivasi akan berlangsung otomatis, tunggu saja hingga selesai.
Jika sudah selesai dan berhasil, akan muncul keterangan Product activated successfully.
Terakhir, silahkan tutup jendela CMD tersebut karena aktivasi sudah selesai.
Setelah melakukan langkah-langkah aktivasi di atas dan prosesnya berhasil, maka sekarang Laptop Windows 10 anda sekarang telah aktif dan semua fitur sudah bisa digunakan.
Cara ke-2: Aktifkan Windows 10 Menggunakan File Batch
Pastikan Laptop anda konek ke jaringan internet karena ini aktivasi online.
Setelah itu, klik link di bawah ini untuk mendapatkan kode aktivasinya.
Klik kanan pada halaman yang terbuka yang menampilkan kode, lalu klik Save as.
Pada jendela Save As, pilih lokasi dimana anda ingin menyimpan file tersebut, misalnya di Desktop.
Setelah itu, silahkan ubah bagian Save as type menjadi All Files.
Ubah juga File name dan ganti .txt menjadi .bat pada akhiran nama file tersebut.
Setelah semuanya diubah, klik tombol Save untuk menyimpan file batch tersebut.
Selanjutnya, buka File Explorer dan cari dimana file batch tadi tersimpan.
Setelah ketemu, klik kanan pada file batch tersebut, lalu klik Run as administrator.
Jika muncul jendela Windows protected your PC, klik saja More info, lalu klik Run anyway.
Pada jendela User Account Control, klik Yes untuk tetap melanjutkan.
Setelah itu akan terbuka CMD dan proses aktivasi berlangsung otomatis, tunggu hingga selesai.
Jika aktivasi sudah selesai dan berhasil, akan muncul keterangan Product activated successfully.
Terakhir, tutup saja jendela CMD tersebut karena aktivasi sudah selesai.
Sekarang anda sudah bisa menggunakan semua fitur yang ada di Windows 10 tersebut karena sudah teraktivasi.
Solusi Jika Aktivasi Gagal dan Muncul Error
Meskipun anda sudah melakukan langkah-langkah aktivasi dengan benar dan teliti, namun kadang ada saja faktor lain yang membuat aktivasi tidak bisa berjalan lancar dan berujung gagal serta muncul error.
Keterangan error yang sering muncul saat aktivasi menggunakan CMD atau file batch yang gagal adalah Windows Script Host is disabled. Jika anda mendapati error ini, tidak usah panik karena sangat mudah untuk mengatasinya agar aktivasi bisa berhasil.
Penyebab yang paling sering membuat terjadi CScript Error: Windows Script Host access is disabled on this machine, Contact your administrator for details adalah aplikasi Smadav. Aplikasi Smadav memiliki fitur untuk memblokir Windows Script Host, padahal sangat dibutuhkan saat aktivasi.
Jadi, jika pada Laptop Windows 10 anda terdapat aplikasi Smadav, maka sudah pasti aplikasi tersebut biang keroknya. Solusinya, anda harus mengizinkan Windows Script Host, lebih jelasnya ikuti saja panduan pada tutorial cara mengatasi Windows Script Host disabled.
Jika Windows Script Host sudah anda izinkan, maka silahkan ulangi proses aktivasi seperti pada cara yang sebelumnya dilakukan. Karena Windows Script Host sudah diizinkan, maka seharusnya proses aktivasi sudah berjalan lancar dan bisa berhasil.
Mengecek Windows 10 Sudah Aktif atau Belum
Setelah melakukan salah satu cara di atas, maka silahkan anda kembali cek status aktivasi Windows 10 anda, apakah sudah benar-benar aktif atau belum. Anda bisa melakukan pengecekan melalui Windows Settings.
Untuk melakukannya, silahkan klik tombol Start di Windows 10, kemudian klik Settings (icon gerigi). Setelah itu akan terbuka jendela Settings, silahkan klik Update & Security.
Pada halaman selanjututnya yang terbuka, silahkan klik Activation yang ada di bagian sebelah kiri. Setelah itu, akan muncul bagian Activation yang menampilkan status aktivasi Windows 10 anda.
Jika Windows 10 anda sudah benar-benar teraktivasi, maka pada bagian activation akan tertulis keterangan Windows is activated. Itu artinya bahwa sekarang watermark Activate Windows sudah hilang dan semua fitur Windows 10 sudah bisa digunakan, termasuk mengubah pengaturan personalisasi.
Tapi, jika ternyata status Windows 10 anda belum teraktivasi, maka silahkan anda mengulangi salah satu cara aktivasi di atas. Pastikan bahwa anda mengikuti semua langkah dengan benar agar proses aktivasinya berhasil.
Cek Masa Aktif Windows 10, Permanen atau Tidak
Setelah Laptop anda berhasil teraktivasi, maka tidak ada salahnya anda juga memeriksa masa aktifnya. Anda bisa melakukan pengecekan masa aktif tersebut untuk mengetahui apakah Windows 10 anda teraktivasi permanen atau ada masa expirednya.
Secara umum, jika anda melakukan aktivasi menggunakan lisensi original, maka Laptop Windows 10 anda akan teraktivasi permanen. Namun, jika anda melakukan aktivasi menggunakan file batch atau CMD, maka Windows 10 tersebut hanya akan aktif selama 180 hari atau 6 bulan.
Untuk mengetahui lebih jelas sampai kapan masa aktifnya, anda bisa mengikuti panduan pada tutorial cara cek masa aktif Windows 10. Dengan melakukan pengecekan, anda bisa mengetahui apakah Windows 10 di Laptop anda aktif permanen atau hanya 6 bulan.
Namun, tidak usah khawatir karena meskipun Windows 10 anda hanya aktif selama 6 bulan, anda tetap bisa menggunakan Windows 10 tersebut sampai kapanpun. Tapi, anda harus melakukan proses aktivasi ulang jika masa aktif Windows 10 anda sudah habis.
Dengan kata lain, jika anda ingin terus menggunakan Windows 10 yang teraktivasi, maka anda harus melakukan aktivasi setiap 6 bulan sekali. Tentu saja ini tidaklah merepotkan karena proses aktivasinya sangat mudah dan cuma butuh waktu beberapa menit untuk menyelesaikannya.
Penutup
Demikian beberapa cara aktivasi Windows 10 home, pro, education dan enterprise secara gratis tanpa product key. Anda bisa melakukan aktivasi gratis tanpa software pakai CMD maupun file batch.
Jadi, jika saat ini Windows 10 anda tidak aktif dan tidak punya product key original, maka silahkan gunakan salah satu cara di atas untuk mengaktifkannya. Setelah aktivasi berhasil, maka anda bisa menggunakan semua fitur Windows 10 yang ada di Laptop.
